utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. I was told that there's something you want to raise, Mr. Tieger, or Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Your Honours, unfortunately we -- the next witness, Dr. Mirsad Mujadzic is not ready to commence his testimony this morning due to circumstances beyond his control. He didn't arrive in The Hague until yesterday afternoon, at which point I met him very briefly and then he was to review his Stakic testimony, and he was unable to do that due to jet lag. He has still around 70 per cent of the cross-examination to review, which he's doing right now. I would think that we could start him at 11.00 a.m. I think he would be completed the review of that testimony at that point. Unfortunately, we also do not have the next witness here, because he was due to be brought at around two and a half hours into this morning. So if Your Honours -- we could either ask VWS to bring the next witness, KDZ-163, but we probably wouldn't be able to start him before 10.00 a.m., and then we would have to stop him to start Dr. Mujadzic, because he actually has professional obligations and he needs to return to the country where he resides tomorrow afternoon. Mr. Tieger wants to add something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That means we have -- we may have to lose one or -- one hour or even two hours at the least.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was going to mention in terms of the option between rushing the next witness over and trying to start a bit early or just commencing with this witness at approximately 11.00. Apparently there's a small fortuity involvement. I spoke with Mr. Robinson earlier. There's apparently -- the Defence is apparently having some difficulty with printing documents that they needed for the cross-examination, and so there seem to be some benefit to simply the -- commencing -- waiting and commence with this witness at approximately 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The document he is currently reviewing, it's the Stakic transcript which is intended to be tendered as his Rule 92 ter statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. He has approximately 140 pages to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is originally of 300-something pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given, then Mr. -- I'm speaking purely for myself, but given then Mr. Tieger was able to lead the previous witness, whose original Rule 92 ter statement was of 734 pages in two and a half hours, can the witness not be led live in two hours' time just now instead of waiting for him to read his transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to clarify, I don't want that to be a case of no good deed goes unpunished. That approach would not have been possible with -- without the period of time in between the Court's order and at least one very, very long night preparing the examination-in-chief so it could be efficient. I'm quite confident that had I simply been obligated to start without such consideration and preparation the examination would have been quite inefficient and very lengthy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for information, witnesses order as it stands now is Dr. Mujadzic, and next one is who?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: KDZ-163, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then comes Mr. Krejic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any observation, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not at the moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I, concerning the length of the allocated time for the cross? I didn't consult Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I will speak Serbian. I'm sorry. With all due respect, I have to say that I really believe that the integrity of the process has been threatened. This witness testified only in Stakic for two days in examination-in-chief and over one day in cross-examination. The entire cross-examination is not included in 92 ter, and you have given me only two and a half hours to cross-examine him, and he was a very important participant, and besides, the Prosecutor has included a lot of political topics that probably need to be discussed with this witness because he was a politician. But really, I can't even discuss a single interview of his where he explains his role in only two and a half hours that were given to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I respond to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The cross -- the cross-examination was 170 pages. The -- sorry, the examination-in-chief was 170 pages plus 4 pages of re-examination. The cross-examination was 149 pages. So it was just a little bit less than the examination-in-chief, and the questions by the Court were 10 pages. The entire cross-examination is included. Mr. -- Dr. Mujadzic was cross-examined on a number of documents including statements made by him by the Defence counsel in the Stakic case. That is all covered. If Mr. Karadzic has got something in addition that he wishes to cross-examine the witness on then it's for him to do that in the time that the Court's allocated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we cannot have the luxury of putting every point to every witness. We considered all the circumstances and formed the view that two and a half hours would be sufficient. This may be a good example that you can show us that you can prioritise your questions and focus on important matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will rise and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, may I -- may I just say a word? The cross-examination that Ms. Sutherland is referring to happened in the proceedings where a wonderful man was given life at the end of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber has given its ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I actually think there might be a problem concerning this witness, because I noticed that what was uploaded into e-court and what Dr. Karadzic and I read as the transcript was 246 pages and did not include all of the cross-examination or the redirect examination, and now I just checked e-court and now there's 333 pages. So think that the Prosecution may have initially not -- not had all of the transcript uploaded into e-court, and as a result both Dr. Karadzic and I haven't read the entire testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: May I respond, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Mujadzic's testimony has been disclosed to the Defence for a long, long time under Rule 66(A)(ii). Now, I don't know -- I don't understand the glitch with e-court, and I can check that, but in any event, it was disclosed quite some time ago pursuant to the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, we -- when we got the 92 ter notification, I opened up the e-court number that they represented would be the 92 ter material, and it had -- I downloaded it. I have it on my computer. It's 246 pages. It ends at a particular day with the cross-examination in the middle. Now I see that they have 333 pages up. Maybe in some batch of the 2 million pages that we've been given, there is another complete package of the Stakic transcript, but I think we're entitled to rely on the 92 ter notice for what is going to be used in court and that's what we did. We don't have the resources to go back and see everything is included.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll leave at it that. It's that the Prosecution is minded to tender the Stakic transcript in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That was going to be my point, Your Honour. In the 92 ter notification we filed six weeks ago, it actually said the transcript pages and it included the entire transcript of the Stakic testimony, and it said from the 27th of May until the 30th of May, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's leave it. But it's a separate matter for the Prosecution to make sure that in the -- to upload everything at any time in complete forms. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take -- make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Mujadzic, and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Could you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Mirsad, also known as Mirza, Mujadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What are your professional qualifications?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I'm a physician.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Are you currently practising as a physician?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As we discussed, part of your evidence in this case is going to be submitted in writing, and we first need to deal with the formalities associated with that submission. You've testified in a number of ICTY trials, and in particular the Stakic trial, on -- between the 27th and the 30th of May, 2002. You've now had the opportunity to review those Stakic transcripts. Do these transcripts accurately reflect your statements at the time, and that if asked about the same matters here in court, you would provide the same information?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender 22183A which is the witness's Stakic testimony, and also 22183B which is a public redacted version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What does the redaction pertain to?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would have to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit both versions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter number 22183A will be Exhibit P3702 under seal, and 65 ter number 22183B will be 3703.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With Your Honours' leave, I will read a short summary of the witness's evidence. The witness is a medical doctor by profession. From 1990 onwards, the witness held various positions within the Party of Democratic Action, that is, the SDA. He was president of the SDA in Prijedor and held the position of president of the SDA Regional Board in Banja Luka. He was also a member of the Chamber called the Council of Citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the latter capacity, he participated in political events on the republic level. Dr. Mujadzic testified about the disintegration of the former Yugoslavia and the ethnic tension in the region resulting from it. He testified as to the political developments in BiH and Prijedor in 1991 and 1992. The witness testified about the ethnic make-up and the relations between the ethnic groups in the Prijedor municipality during the relevant time. He also testified about the policies pursued by the SDS and its relations with other political parties in the Prijedor municipality. He addressed the political structures of the SDS and the establishment of Serb local bodies. Dr. Mujadzic described the negotiations of the SDA representatives with members of the SDS party in relation to positions, power sharing, and proposals to avoid conflict, including his participation in these talks. He testified to a conversation he had with Stojan Zupljanin regarding the situation in the Prijedor police. The witness testified about the communication between local SDS structures and those on the republic level and described a conversation he had with Radovan Karadzic on the negotiations in Prijedor. In his capacity as a member of the council of citizens, he observed Mr. Karadzic in the BiH Assembly sessions. The witness testified about a meeting he had with General Momir Talic in Sanski Most in April 1992. He described the Serb takeover of power in Prijedor on the 29th and 30th of April, 1992, and also an incident at Hambarine check-point the day before the shelling of Hambarine in late May 1992. Shortly after the attack on Hambarine, the witness fled to the nearby Kurevo forest where he stayed until around 27 June 1992 when he left the Prijedor area and escaped on foot to Bihac. Dr. Mujadzic also spoke about the persecution of non-Serbs including the detention and killing of several of his relatives in the Omarska detention facility. That completes the summary of the witness's written evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Mujadzic, did you know Radoslav Brdjanin from parliament?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What position did he have in parliament?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: He was an MP in the Council of Municipalities. I believe that that was the name of the body, the Council of Municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you have any contacts with him during parliament sittings?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was nothing official. Those were our regular contacts, conversations in passing when we came across each other in the hallway. We did not really have any official contacts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What, if anything, did he say to you about the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: He thought and he said it publicly, and it was not a result of my conversation with him. He stated that in the Banja Luka region there were too many Bosniaks and that their numbers should be reduced to perhaps 2, 3 per cent. He even made some bad jokes about that. He stated that a few Muslims should be left behind to make cevapi, which is a Bosnian speciality. I found that in poor taste.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And do you recall when Brdjanin said this, made these remarks?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the date, but I know that that was after the setting up of the Autonomous Region of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you say Autonomous Region of Banja Luka or Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I said Banja Luka, and I meant Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also testified that at some point steps were -- some steps were undertaken with the TO to organise some form of defence. When did -- when did those steps begin?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the time period. If we are talking only about the Territorial Defence, I believe that we started thinking about that sometime after the putsch in Prijedor. That would have been after the 30th of April. We tried to come up with other ways. In addition to the Territorial Defence, we also considered the defence of the entire region and which parts of the region could be defended, and that applied only to the left bank of the Sana River. If that's the part of my testimony in the previous cases, in Brdjanin and Stakic cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At page 3649 and 3650 -- or at page 3649, you were questioned about hearing Mr. Karadzic at an Assembly session making certain remarks about the road down which you are headed, and at that point you were asked about conversations you may have had with any individuals in order to -- the possibility to prepare the people or the Bosniaks or non-Serbs, the population -- to protect the population, and you said that you did take certain steps at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you ever contemplate offensive actions against the JNA, against the SDS, or Serb citizens in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Leading. Leading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Mujadzic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh. It's moot then. Shall we deal with associate exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Except for those that have already been admitted, I note that one of the exhibit -- document has been already admitted. You noted 65 ter 1461 -- 631. I can't find it in e-court, and it says it's a duplicate of 65 ter 21285 which has been admitted as Exhibit P3536. Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I can't find that on the Rule 92 ter notification. Could you please direct me to the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have my own notation that -- I don't have with me the original notification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's on the bottom of the second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I see that. Yes, that's already exhibited, there are a couple of others that have also been exhibited recently since the filing of the Rule 92 ter notification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you identify them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That is 65 ter number 05745 is now P03529.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 65 ter number, two documents down from that one that I just mentioned, 65 ter number 05473. The witness was -- was taken to the first decision in that official gazette which is -- has its own 65 ter number 05438, which is now Exhibit P02818.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is that 65 ter number originally?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 05438 just for that first decision in the official gazette of all of the conclusions of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then further down 65 ter number 20961 is a Defence exhibit D00400, but it's -- it's simply -- it's a different version of the one that -- that we have in 65 ter number 20961, but the document, the Delimustafic document dated the 29th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say 20961?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's the third-to-last exhibit on the list of associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then the -- the one directly below that, 20192, was exhibited very recently and that is D01831.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And with respect to 65 ter numbers 21285 to 21287 and 21288, what did the witness say about those documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, not a great deal, and in 21287, he simply identified Stakic's signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the Chamber's view, those three documents do not form the part -- indispensable and inseparable part of the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In relation to 21285, that's already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: There's also ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you tell us the number, exhibit number? 21285?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, P03536. You actually mentioned it earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in relation to 21288, we don't seek to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. And you won't tender 21287 either.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. And lastly, the video, 65 ter number which was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since we were not provided with the video earlier on, we -- we can't know how much of the video was shown to the witness and what part of the video you're tendering.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just about to give you the time-code for that and that is 00:25:77 to 00:39:08. So it's a matter of a few seconds -- more than a few seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any objections otherwise, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then all those associated exhibits will be admitted into evidence and be given numbers. Very well. Dr. Mujadzic, your testimony in the Stakic case was admitted in its entirety into evidence in this case in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you are -- you will be further examined by Mr. Karadzic in his cross-examination. Mr. Karadzic, are you ready? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Mujadzic.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I must say that this will take even more time because technical means are not working. I can simply not print my own materials. We've been working on that but the job is still pending, so it will all be slowed down by the fact that I couldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you shared with us what Brdjanin told you only today. Why didn't [Realtime transcript read in error "Detention Unit"] you say that publicly before the Assembly so that Brdjanin may be admonished for what he said?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin said that publicly, and besides me, many other public figures heard that, including politicians and citizens. I was not the only one who heard his statement. The information even reached Sarajevo and judicial and enforcement bodies. It was a public statement. Everybody heard that. So it was not my exclusive responsibility to launch an initiative for Mr. Brdjanin to be admonished or punished for his political statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt, but I do need to clarify this. This is not the first time Dr. Mujadzic has mentioned this. He said it in his Brdjanin testimony at transcript page 13306.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, I did not claim that it was absolutely the first time he said it today. My question was why he did not present that issue before the Assembly, which was the only legitimate body that could consider that. Why didn't somebody file a criminal report? Why didn't he file a criminal report? Because if it was said in a serious tone, it should have been subject to a prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that -- was that a question for me, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is just my response to Madam Sutherland and a clarification of my question. I didn't say this was the first time you mentioned this. I just thought that this should have been dealt with in time if it had been said seriously, if it was not a joke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just before we go further, I'm just wondering whether the transcript is correct when -- just second. It's page 16, lines 6 and 7. Did you mention the detention unit? "Why Detention Unit say that publicly before the Assembly so that Brdjanin may be admonished?"

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think it's, "Why did you not say that publicly," perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything is bad. I didn't say this was the first time he said. I asked why those things were not said publicly, why Brdjanin was not prosecuted for what he said, why the issue wasn't raised before the Assembly. If it was said seriously, he should have lost his office as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Karadzic is making comment. If he can put a question to Dr. Mujadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that this is the -- this is a question for Dr. Mujadzic. Can you answer the question, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was just one of the deputies in parliament, and I had no political or any other prerogatives to put that in motion. There were many more politically responsible and other individuals who could have set that in motion, so I can't really answer why that wasn't done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Mujadzic, today you repeated, and I believe that you've said this in your earlier testimony as well, that my speech of the 15th of October, 1991, when our deputies walked out of the parliament, you said that that address of mine was a warning to you and that it was a -- something that told you that you should start with defence preparations.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I really said that, and I didn't mean the speech, that address before the parliament. I was talking about the global and general situation and the tendencies at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, if I had the materials that I need printed out, I would be able to give you a reference, but let me remind you. You said and you interpreted a speech of mine. You said that I said you were not ready for war yet. So let me remind you of this: In this speech that the Trial Chamber is familiar with, I was urging you not to go the path of war and force and secession because that would lead to hell. And I said at that time that the Muslims could not defend themselves, finding themselves between Serbs and Croats, and I paraphrase Mr. Filipovic who had earlier said at the earlier session the following words: If these policies should continue my nation will disappear. And as I had been on good terms with Mr. Filipovic, he had asked me not to quote him because then he would be subject to attack. So my thesis was not that this should not be done but that you wouldn't be able to defend yourselves in case war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, let me just clarify something. The speech you referred to and you're talking about the 15th of October, 1991, whereas I believe that the address that you would like to refer to is something that happened later in the Assembly. I don't think it was on the 15th of October, 1991. I think, rather, that that speech of yours was related to the referendum which would have been later, in 1992, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you are right in one sense. I did address the parliament in -- on the 25th of January, 1992, when Mr. Cengic and I - and this transcript has been admitted into evidence here - Mr. Cengic and I spoke. We came out together, and we proposed that this referendum be postponed until regionalisation was put in place and in that event the Serbs would also vote in the referendum and it would be legitimate. However, the disappearance of one of the ethnicities, that was something that was mentioned in October, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The 15th of October, 1995 [sic]?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that your speech in the Assembly was then. I believe that that was later, Mr. Karadzic. If we mean the same speech, the speech in which you said what you've just mentioned now, that the Muslims would be unable to defend themselves, the Bosniaks would be unable to defend themselves in a war should it break out and that in that case our option if we were continue that path would just lead to hell and eventually lead to the disappearance of Bosniaks. If you're referring to that speech, I think that was -- that came much later than October 1991 and I would appreciate it if someone knows this as a fact. Perhaps they can help us so we can determine, establish when exactly this speech was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You can be sure that it was on the 15th of October?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I remember you rose.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to clarify the answer the witness gave as to the date in the transcript, page 19, line 15, it says the 15th of October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I don't know if Mr. Karadzic wants to clarify that with the witness as to the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The speech that I am referring to and we have already admitted it into evidence here and I believe we've already also seen a video, video footage of it, was on the 15th of October, 1991. That was when our deputies walked out and do you remember, Dr. Mujadzic, that on the 24th of October we established an Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this was precisely because of the walkout on the 15th of October.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let me ask you this: Is it correct that you as a national entity, as an ethnic entity, actually waged war against Serbs, against Croats, and even against parts of the Muslim ethnicity, the Abdic followers in the Cazin Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't really put it that way, Mr. Karadzic. We didn't wage war on Serbs or Croats or Muslims. We defended Bosnia-Herzegovina from those who were putting it in jeopardy. Not all Serbs were putting Bosnia-Herzegovina in jeopardy, not all Croats, or all Muslims. And I'm sure you know that there were quite a few Serbs in the Bosnian ranks of the Bosnian Army, as well as Croats, and that there were a number of deputies of Serb ethnicity who remained throughout the war members of the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The same is true of Croats. And this up to the highest levels of power including the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including Tatjana Lujic Mijatovic, for instance, who was a member of the Presidency of Serb ethnicity. In other words, we never waged war on Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, my apologies, but I haven't been given enough time so please let's not try to joust here politically. Now, did you defend Bosnia from some Serbs, some Croats, and some Muslims where you fought the Serbs for three years, Muslims for one, and Croats for one year? So did you actually wage three wars?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Well, these were three different series of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But tell us what was this war about? In what sense did you -- or were you defending Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: We were defending Bosnia from aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, tell us, please, am I correct? Bosnia as we have it today, the Dayton Bosnia, was never in dispute -- or, rather, from the moment that we accepted Bosnia's independence, in other words, Bosnia was not defending itself. It wasn't a fight for the freedom and independence of Bosnia. Rather, it was a fight other whether it would be a unified unitary Bosnia or not.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, there were negotiations before the Dayton Accords where there were attempts to regionalise Bosnia and Herzegovina, and if you recall, I believe there was an agreement with Lord Carrington and there were several such agreements, actually, where attempts were made to regionalise Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to come up with a political solution and find a compromise, and I believe there were a number of negotiations on that issue, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this is an entire new set of questions so I have no time to go into that, but the fact remains, doesn't it, would you agree, that the Serbs were in favour of remaining within Yugoslavia; that was the first option. The second priority was for the Serbian parts to remain within Yugoslavia. And the third option or rather concession was to accept an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina within its existing borders on condition that we get our own constituent entity; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I could agree with the two first statements you made, or theses. It is true that the SDS insisted on Bosnia remaining in Yugoslavia, and it is true that the SDS insisted on those parts of Bosnia where the Serbs had a majority to remain in some kind of administrative connection with Yugoslavia, but I don't recall that the Serbian Democratic Party ever supported, under any conditions, an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. I wish to God we had such negotiations. Perhaps we could have come up with some kind of solution in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, this wasn't really a question. What I'm -- what you've -- what we see in the transcript is another question that's not really a question. That's part of the answer. Now, Dr. Mujadzic, let me just remind you. My address in the Assembly together with Mr. Cengic on the 25th of January had to do with the referendum and that the Serbs would remain and take part in the referendum if the government agreed to regionalisation before that. So already at that time we were accepting an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, but can you tell me, was that the first time that there was agreement that Bosnia would remain independent and then up until the 18th of March this thesis was being worked on and almost finalised. The only issues that remain to be cleared up were some issues relating to the armed forces and some adjustments to the maps; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Well, of course I remember.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what agreement exactly he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Dr. Mujadzic, because both of you are speaking the same language which should be interpreted into English and French, I would appreciate it very much if you could put a pause before you start answering. In any event, the interpreters couldn't follow your response, so could you kindly repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. I will try to make a pause before I actually begin answering to give enough time to interpreters to do their job. So let me repeat what I've said in answer. Mr. Karadzic, I do remember that you talked with Cengic, and of course I remember the Lisbon agreement, and I remember the proposal for regionalisation that was included in the agreement. The only thing that I honestly cannot recall is that detail that the Serbian Democratic Party ever accepted an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina under any conditions. I'm not saying that's not the case, but I can't remember that. Would you have -- could you point out some detail in order to corroborate that? And of course if I see such a document of course I would accept your claim. In other words, I'm not saying that what you're claiming is not correct, it's just that I do not remember it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We do have evidence and exhibits on that, but I've already said that part of the Lisbon agreement was that Bosnia and Herzegovina was accepted by Serbs within the existing borders, and we wanted some ties with Yugoslavia. Now, can you tell me --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does Dr. Mujadzic -- Dr. Mujadzic, do you stand by what you've said in your earlier testimony that this speech of mine was a warning light that you realized that you should then start your preparations for war and that it was only then that you started preparing for war?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: We began some more serious thinking about how to defend Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time, because after that speech of yours, we were forewarned. We were also reminded of some facts, and your statement was absolutely true. We were totally unarmed. We were not organised, and we had absolutely no chance for any kind of defence at that point in time. It was zero. In other words, after those words of yours, that was just a reminder to us what the factual situation was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My apologies but that was not my question. My question was had you already embarked on preparations for war even before that or was it only from that point onwards?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: At this time, we gave some serious thought to the defences of Bosnia and Herzegovina and what our capabilities were. True, there were some earlier thoughts about that, about what to do with in the event of some political difficulties that might result in an aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina, because we had already seen what would happen in Slovenia and Croatia, and of course we were aware completely that the political developments could bring Bosnia and Herzegovina into similar situation, and of course it is true that there was already some thinking about some action that needed to be taken in terms of defence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have 1D2906 in e-court, and I need page 8. Could we please zoom in on the left bottom part of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a series of articles, an interview with you, in the New Mirror, "Novo Ogledalo," of March 1995, and let me read it: [As read] "And then when all -- when there is no more room for political dialogue, then what follows is an armed conflict, and prompted by this I invited some of my colleagues at the Krajina level where we organised already in early January 1991, we held a first meeting where we analysed the possible consequences of the further evolution in that direction. And it was our conclusion then that war was inexorably coming closer and we should start preparing for defence at that time, and I would like to stress out that it never occurred us to that we should be the ones to initiate conflict, that we should do anything politically or in any other way to provoke the other side. We simply understood that the way the events were going, they were going against our wishes and our commitments. In other words, a month after the election" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note that only partially it has been translated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is possible, because we used the second part with another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question is whether why it's not uploaded. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether this part was translated; it should have maybe. But Excellency, really, we are under such pressure that the Defence feels disabled in many ways. Everybody admits that this is a mega-trial but nothing else is mega. Everything else is average; the number of people working on this case, the resources that I have, so if it's a mega-trial then there should be a mega-defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's not spend our time on those issues. That has already been addressed and discussed. Not now. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Mujadzic, you said that already a month after we jointly established the new democratic government you started preparations for organising a defence; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I've just confirmed what I've already said to you, and I said that in greater detail in my statement in the Tadic case. I explained in detail why I had come to such a conclusion. It was not a personal conclusion on my part; it was the conclusion of other people. If Their Honours allow me to, I will mention a few things that led me to think along those lines. However, I would also like to point out that what I said here was that we did not want to provoke the other side in any way. We were not the ones who were destroying Yugoslavia. That is what this text says further on. We were in favour of peace and preserving Yugoslavia at all costs, and Mr. Izetbegovic and all of us from the SDA made a huge effort to preserve Yugoslavia, because we realized that the Bosniaks would be the greatest losers if there were to be a conflict or a war, and that is why we tried to avoid any possibility of a war, and we made all kinds of concessions to the other side in order to avoid that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Dr. Mujadzic, these are reasons that I'm not challenging. However, I am interested in a fact. In January 1991, did you have these meetings? And just look further on. In Velika Kladusa, you had a meeting, and there's this question here. How about showing the middle part on our screens now. Mujadzic says this meeting was held sometime in mid-January 1991 in Kladusa. There it is, question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not denying that. The elections were held in September, and from September until January was four or five months, and many things happened. Let me just summarise briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, please don't justify what you did. I'm not challenging that. These were your rights. But weren't the elections held on the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I think that the elections were held earlier, Mr. Karadzic, if -- they were a bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 18th of November. All right. That can be checked easily. Tell us, please, did you, I mean you the Muslim community, did you take steps to establish this Patriotic League, and did you make a decision to that effect on the 30th of March, and did you actually establish it on the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the 30th of April, 1991, is the date from which years of service in the BH Army are recognised according to BH law, two different individuals.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll have a look at this, but I want to say that this is spelled out in the law now, that that is when the defence forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina came into being. Is it correct that Sefer Halilovic came to see you in Prijedor in order to take care of that precisely, the establishment of the Patriotic League in September 1991, for instance, before my speech?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it already in September --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow to which question the witness said, "Yes," because you ask so many questions. Dr. Mujadzic, yes to which question? That you met Mr. Halilovic in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that all, or -- or whether you answered positively that he raised the issue of Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer was yes, meaning that Mr. Halilovic was in Prijedor. However, the answer is no when he said that the Muslim community raised the issue of the Patriotic League. That is what I said was incorrect, but it is correct that Mr. Halilovic came. Mr. Karadzic is constructing certain things through his questions. The Muslim community is a concept that I'm unaware of. I know that there is the Islamic community but I don't know what this Muslim community is. The Patriotic League was an initiative of Sefer Halilovic, a personal initiative of his. He never belonged to the SDA. He was never a member of the SDA. The Patriotic League was supported by the Party of Democratic Action, but there were members who had nothing whatsoever to do with the Patriotic League, and the Patriotic League was a defence front. There was no direct link with the Party of Democratic Action. The Party of Democratic Action was just one of the parties that supported such activities, because they considered the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina to be an objective fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You're a remarkable speaker, and it would be wonderful to listen to you, but let us deal with specific questions now. Is it correct that Sefer Halilovic came to see you in Prijedor in September 1991 to work on the establishment of the Patriotic League in Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've already answered that question in the affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With which Serb representatives did he discuss the establishment of the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not sure whether he had discussions with some people. At the time, Sefer Halilovic was outside the system of the SDA. He had the right and freedom to do whatever he wanted. Now, whether he talked to some persons who were of Serb ethnicity, I don't know. I don't know whether that happened in Prijedor. I know that he did that in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I know, for sure, that some members of the Patriotic League were ethnic Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From whom was he given this total freedom to do whatever he wanted?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Each and every citizen in Bosnia-Herzegovina - it was a free state at the time - had the right to start any kind of initiative, especially if that initiative was patriotic, in a patriotic sense. So this was personal initiative of Mr. Sefer Halilovic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Sefer Halilovic who left the JNA decided to establish a military organisation with a military staff, with a civilian staff, a political staff, and he could do that in full accordance with the law as he prepared the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina while sidestepping the Serbs and I think the Croat representatives as well, the official representatives.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that, Mr. Karadzic. Have you ever read the platform of the Patriotic League? If you've read the platform of the Patriotic League, then you can see from the platform that it is broad based and that it involves potentially all citizens who support Bosnia-Herzegovina and that there is no reference to the Party of Democratic Action in that platform. Also, there is no exclusive mention of the Bosniak community, the Muslim community, whatever you wish. The Patriotic League had a very broad-based platform, and it included all patriots who supported Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that these meetings were public meetings, that they were followed by the media as well?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know to what extent this was given publicity. I don't think it was exactly public at the time. It was the JNA that was still the official army in the area. In my previous speeches, I explained why such initiatives had been initiated. In Croatia, the JNA had already acted as the de facto Serb army, although de jure was still the Yugoslav army. Your Honours, sorry, may I just explain this. For me, Yugoslavia means all citizens of the former Yugoslavia of all ethnic and religious backgrounds. At the moment when the war was underway in Croatia, the JNA was practically a Serb army exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, in the top echelons of that army, and we don't have enough time to deal with it now, there was Anton Tus, a Croat. The minister of defence was a half Croat, half Serb from Croatia. The head of the air force was a Croat. The deputy chief of General Staff was a Slovene, Brovet. So there were many of them. So most of these people who were in the highest positions of responsibility were non-Serbs, but let's leave that aside, Doctor. This is what I'm interested in only: Do you remember actually --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D264 can we have that called up?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you mean that Izetbegovic, Kljuic, and I constantly worked on monitoring the situation and making efforts to ease tensions and that we sent you instructions on the establishment of mixed groups that were to follow any increases in these tensions that should be reported back? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that agreement. However, as for the implementation of such activities on the ground, there was no adequate co-operation on the part of the Serb Democratic Party. I've already explained that in my previous statements. Even in the election campaign this co-operation was refused by the SDS in Prijedor, because our party called for co-operation, co-operation from the SDS and the HDZ. However, such activities were adamantly refused by the SDS in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't have time to go into each and every minute detail. Did you delegate, if I can put it that way, your own members in order to establish these groups that would supervise -- or, rather, monitor things that were happening and then report back to their own headquarters? The 27th of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. I think that we had some preliminary talks with the representatives of the SDS and the HDZ along those lines, but I think that as for the implementation of this agreement it was never actually carried through. Unfortunately, I know that no such agreement functioned on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Right now on 3571, plus 15, my technical equipment doesn't seem to be working --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: 3586, possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are saying -- and I thank you for that. You are talking about Ustasha crimes in the Second World War and you admit that Serbs had this reflex. Well, that's not exactly the way that you put it, but that they had cause for concern. Now, what does it say here? Line 16. I'll read it in English so that they interpret it better. [As read] "[In English] From the historical point of view until 1942 Prijedor was controlled by so-called Ustasha government. This was the government of the Independent State of Croatia and its dictator, Ante Pavelic. It was a time in which particularly the Serb people suffered a great deal of damage and loss of lives, especially from Potkozarje. Many Serbs from Potkozarje perished in the camp at Jasenovac. So that's -- that's the way Serbs from the region perceived the situation from a position full of pain in terms of Second World War." [Interpretation] So you are not mocking these victims.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not. I'm aware of the history of that area, and the fact that I referred to all of this guided our relations with the Serbian Democratic Party. You do remember, Mr. Karadzic, that there was is this initiative of the Prijedor Bosniak intellectuals during the Second World War. This initiative was signed by 86 Bosniaks from Prijedor and it was sent to Ante Pavelic asking to stop the persecution of the Serbs and you also know that many Bosniaks defended and protected many Serbs, even Srdjo Srdic, who was president of the SDS in Prijedor was protected by Bosniaks from Kozarac. His family was supposed to be killed including himself. He was a child at the time. However they were taken out of Prijedor, protected, so Srdjo Srdic who was at the time president of the SDS always referred to that, saying that that showed the good co-operation between the Bosniaks and Serbs in Prijedor during the Second World War. Of course, we took this into account, and we tried in every possible way to have the Serb people in the area of Prijedor know that our position is still the same, namely that we want to have good relations with the Serb people in that area and that of course if anything were to happen again, we would again protect the Serb people as we did in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you about this because we have witnesses appearing here who say that they laugh when we mention Serbs victims in the Sana River valley, and I thank you for not doing that. And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not catch the page reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that all parties were against the policy of the Serb Democratic Party and then today you said to us that many Serbs stayed in parliament and so on and so forth, and this is what I'm going to put to you now, I'll put our position to you now about the facts involved. Is it correct that, in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, among different political parties there were 86 Serbs, 72 Serb MPs were in the SDS and 14 were in other political parties. If you don't know, can you take my word for it? It can be checked. That's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I assume that your figure is correct. I'm not exactly sure of the number, but I believe that that was the case. If that is what you say, it does correspond to what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that of the 86 MPs, 83 were members of the Serbian Assembly and that the Assembly still has that number of MPs in memory of the first composition of the Assembly, 83 out of 86 made up the Serbian Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I didn't know that. However, I'm sure that that can be checked very easily. We can very easily find out how many Serbian MPs remained in the parliament when the SDS walked out. I believe that the number was more than 3 Serb MPs, but I don't have any arguments to support my belief. As I said, I believe that that argument can easily be checked. There are documents issued by the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and minutes. It can be easily checked how many Serb MPs remained after the SDS walked out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 1835 [as interpreted], plus 18 -- 3571 plus 18, you speak about the reasons for which Yugoslavia had broken up, and you say that the main reason was the appearance of Milosevic and his request for the voting according to the principle: One person, one vote. Do you know that the first major separatist movement happened in Croatia in 1970 and 1971 and that it ended up in the shakeups and in Kosovo it was in 1986?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, if you are referring to Savka Dapcevic, of course, I remember. Of course I was still a child but I remember subsequent comments about those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that Mr. Milosevic and you claim that we supported him, that he always supported our opponents in any -- in every elections? The first time he supported Ilic, the second time, Radisic, the third time Mladen Ivanic, and the fourth time Biljana Plavsic, but only then when she had turned against the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I cannot provide any comments as regards the relationship between Milosevic and the SDS. I don't think I know enough about those relations in order to provide any comments. I'm not sure that I'm familiar with this photo, Mr. Karadzic, but if you claim that that was the fact and if you have support for your arguments, I don't have a reason not to believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask you this -- actually, I would like to put certain things to you because I don't have enough time to go into any detail. I'm putting to you that there were two original proposals tabled by the Muslim side and directed at the Serbs with regard to the future of Bosnia. The first proposal was by Mr. Izetbegovic, who told us that Bosnia should be independent but that it should consist of three parts. The second proposal was by Mr. Zulfikarpasic, the leader of another Muslim party, for Bosnia to be unitarian, that Serbs should -- Serb should give up on regionalisation but that Bosnia should remain in Yugoslavia. Do you know that we accepted both proposals that, we both -- both those proposals?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I assume that in the first part of your question you were referring to the Lisbon agreement. Is that correct, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Even before that, Dr. Mujadzic. In the month of May, Mr. Izetbegovic tabled a proposal for Bosnia to be divided. We were taken by surprise. You can see that from my telephone conversation with Milosevic that is already on file here. And then can we look what Mr. Zulfikarpasic had to say about that in his book. I would like to call up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one by one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, what's the question that Mr. Karadzic is putting to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Can you now answer the question? The previous question, whether the Serbs admitted both proposals.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first part of the question dealing with the Bosniak proposal about the division of Bosnia into three parts, the only proposal that I remember in that sense was the proposal or the draft of the Lisbon agreement. I don't remember. Mr. Izetbegovic never mentioned before us that he had talks with members of the SDS. The only thing that we were aware of were negotiations leading to the Lisbon agreement that were public. So, Mr. Karadzic, I am not aware of any such agreement. As for the second part of your question, Zulfikarpasic and Muhamed Filipovic's proposal for Bosnia to remain in Yugoslavia, we supported that proposal, Mr. Karadzic. You will remember that the SDA, in its statute, had an element -- one of its main elements is the preservation of Yugoslavia. The SDA was absolutely in favour of the preservation of Yugoslavia for reasons known to you. There were a lot of Bosniaks living in Sandzak and other parts of Croatia and in other parts of Yugoslavia and it was in our best interests for Yugoslavia to remain integral, for two reasons: The first reason was the fact that we knew that if Yugoslavia was to break up that that break-up -- that there was a possibility for the break-up not to be peaceful, and if that came true we could not defend ourselves. And the second reason was that we were politically motivated to preserve Yugoslavia, because Bosniaks, and you know that perfectly well, do not reside only in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have time to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have break for a bit more than 15 minutes and resume at 12.35 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Mujadzic, I will put it to you what the situation looked like from our position. The first idea for a division of Bosnia was put forth to us by Mr. Izetbegovic, and it was not just to us the proposal but also to Mr. Zulfikarpasic and it was first published in the Zagreb Vecernji List, and Mrs. Plavsic commented with the words that it's interesting and that we will review it. Now please take a look at 1D4647. That is from a book by Adil Zulfikarpasic, articles and interviews published in 1991, in late 1991, and this particular article relates to August 1991. So this is the title page. Can we see the second page in e-court, please. Can we zoom in for the benefit of Dr. Mujadzic. Please can you look at what he says here. He speaks about the idea. Maybe you want to read it for us.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: You want me to read the second paragraph which starts on the second page about Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, below that starting with "That idea ..." the third line under the question.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: [As read] "The idea cannot be taken as something real. Alija scared me several times when he said, 'Let the Serbs take what belongs to them. Let Croats take their own, and we will take our own.' It seems that he really accepted the creation of a Muslim conclave if Bosnia was ever to be divided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So not only to us but also to Mr. Zulfikarpasic Alija Izetbegovic presented his idea. We were of the opinion that both ideas were legitimate and honest. If they wanted an independent Bosnia, they should give Serbs at least what they had in Yugoslavia, and if they remain in Yugoslavia, the Serbs would not be entitled to autonomous regions. We accepted both of those ideas in the shape of the Lisbon agreement and in the shape of the historical Serb and Muslim agreement?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Can I take things at a time, Mr. Karadzic. First of all, if we're talking about the Lisbon agreement, I believe it would take us too far and we don't have that much time to look at the reasons why the Lisbon agreement fell through, why the implementation didn't succeed. There are many reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't really like to intervene but what I'm interested in now is this: Did you know that we accepted both ideas and let me also present a third idea to you. The third idea was pushed by Mr. Silajdzic for an independent unitarian Bosnia and this is something that neither us nor Croats could accept, and that's why were at war; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: You want me to answer your last question first about the war and why the war was waged or do you want me to confirm that there were all three ideas on the table?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first question. Do you know that we accepted the first and the second variants? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I personally know only about the Lisbon agreement. I'm not familiar with Zulfikarpasic's book and I didn't know that Mr. Izetbegovic had a conversation with you and talked about the division of Bosnia. I believe that the mood in the general public and the SDA would have been against a division of Bosnia. I believe that people were more in favour of the de-unitarisation of Bosnia and Bosnia remaining within the boundaries with some elements that would be more close to the Lisbon agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you're familiar with the historical Muslim and Serb agreements, so these are the two variants. But do you know that Mr. Izetbegovic signed on the 16th of September, 1993, together with my proxy, Mr. Krajisnik, a declaration according to which the Republika Srpska, if the Muslim side got 33 per cent of the territory, that the Republika Srpska would be entitled to a referendum to vote on its independence?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, can I remind you that in general, the reasons for the war are not relevant for your case. Bear that in mind. As -- as to the specific passage read out in relation to this book, is it something written by Mr. Zulfikarpasic or something written or said by Mr. Maric? Can you help us, Dr. Mujadzic? Because I see the name "Milomir Maric" at the bottom, at the end of this page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally never read this book. However, as I'm looking at the page, I would say that this was an interview with Mr. Zulfikarpasic in which Mr. Milomir Maric conducted the interview. I can only hope that he conveyed the words of Mr. Zulfikarpasic authentically.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance, Your Excellencies, not only were his words conveyed faithfully but Zulfikarpasic actually included that interview in his book, which means that he accepted the interview to be a true reflection of what was said. He included the interview in his book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that you are also minded to tender the witness's newspaper article, which was 1D2906?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellencies, but we'll come back to that interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness wasn't familiar with any of the contents on the page that was just put to him. I don't see a basis for admitting it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to reply, Mr. Robinson, on this issue, Mr. Zulfikarpasic's book?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'll let Dr. Karadzic reply to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zulfikarpasic was one of the main protagonists of the political life in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was the initiator of the second variant which was for Bosnia to remain in Yugoslavia and we give up on regionalisation. He confirms that Mr. Izetbegovic was in favour of the first variant which was the division of Bosnia, a Bosnia outside of Yugoslavia. So this is really relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit the witness's newspaper article, marking it for identification pending full translation. We'll give the number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI'd D1834, Your Honours, and for correction the document admitted on Friday as D1833 -- 1832 will in fact be 1833 which is public redacted version of Exhibit 1523.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I was responding to your question I thought you were wanting my position on this document in front --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm coming to it. And in relation to this, Zulfikarpasic's book, witness has not confirmed anything and I don't think it is relevant or necessary to understand the context or credibility of this witness's evidence. So we'll not admit this at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to go back to the interview again. Is it true that you very early on concluded that it -- it would be very hard to defend Prijedor and that your strategy was to defend the left bank of the Sana river in which a lot of Sanski Most and Bosanski Novi would not be part of the territory you would defend?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: That's correct. With a slight correction here, Mr. Karadzic. That was not my personal plan. That was a plan proposed by people who knew something about strategic defence preparations, who were experts in the area. I, as a political figure, accepted the reality of the situation given the fact that the potential ratio of forces was absolutely negative at our expense -- or, rather, in favour of the other so I accepted that to be the reality, although many in Prijedor and Kozarac did not come to terms with that very easily. But that was the reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I did not mean that that was your personal plan, but that was a plan that you testified about as a position that was taken. Did you say that the plans were hindered by the takeover of parts of the Bosanska Krupa on the right bank of the Una by the Serbs, that that hindered your plan to connect parts between the Una and the Sana with Cazin Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's true I stated that. For the Trial Chamber to be what Mr. Karadzic is talking about, maybe we should show a map to look at the valley of the Una and the valley of the Sana. We should perhaps look at the geographical relations between the two regions and explain why it was believed that the left bank of the Sana was taken as the line that would possibly be defended.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we then briefly see 1D4275, please? This map is painted in different colours for different ethnicities but it will clearly show the positions of all these things that you mentioned so can we have 1D42 -- 4647, please now while we're waiting could we just find out when the strategic plan was -- yes, this is the number we need. So could we please zoom in on the left upper corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mujadzic, when was this plan drafted?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I can't really recall all these events because this was 15, 16 years ago but I do think that it was sometime in late 1991 or early 1992 or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please take a look at this map. We see part of Bihac and all the way up to the Una River we see that on the right-hand side we have Serb areas and to the left are Muslim areas and then we see Prijedor, Sanski Most and Kljuc. They are all on the Sana River; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you could draw a line and we would appreciate the usher to -- the usher's assistance in this. Now, could you just draw the line along the Una River. You are well familiar with it, aren't you? Now, please if you can use a red pen, because that will make it easier to distinguish here. Would you please draw a line along the Una River.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The Una River should be -- well, it runs through Bihac, and then Bosanska Krupa, and then to Bosanski Novi. So this is just a rough sketch. I'm not sure that that this is a very accurate depiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please just put a letter U for Una or number 1.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Here I'll just write down "Una." Now, the Sana River, the source was somewhere near Kljuc. It ran through Kljuc, Sanski Most, Prijedor, and then finally it joined Una at Bosanski Novi. Now, what I described earlier -- or, rather, the plan, the defence plans, was to actually link up Bosanska Krupa, and I will put a dotted line there, with parts of Prijedor and possibly Sanski Most and to try to defend part of the territory of the Krajina on the left-hand side of the Sana River. This would exclude all urban parts of Bosanski Novi, Prijedor, and Sanski Most and Kljuc, because they lay for the most part on the right bank of the Sana. But in any case, there was an obstacle, a geographic obstacle, and this was considered a geographic obstacle by those people who were planning the defence of Bosanska Krajina, and they felt that the only possibility was for the Cazin Krajina, which had a Bosniak majority, that they should assist in this effort. And when Bosanska Krupa was taken by the Serb army, in other words, these lines here, the line was cut off. And the Bosniak Croatian -- or I beg your pardon, Bosniaks, and part of the territory I was referring to, was isolated and any kind of defence would be unsuccessful. The situation was rather desperate, and we knew that that we did not have the capabilities to mount a proper defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please put a CK where the Cazin Krajina is because you mentioned that area for the Trial Chamber, or perhaps you can just draw a circle around it.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: You mean the Bihac region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. You mentioned the word Cazin Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the Bihac region is this entire area, predominantly Muslim, beyond the river --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please put a BR there?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Bihac region, that's BR. Then we have the Sana River which had another densely populated area of Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please put an indication where the Sana is. That's on the right-hand side and the Una is on the left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now can we agree that the Serbs in Bosanska Krupa took control only of the right-hand bank of the Una whereas the left part remained under Muslim control?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Gojko Klickovic, president of the Crisis Staff of Bosanska Krupa was absolved of any responsibility before a Bosnian court?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that detail, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Mujadzic, would you please sign and date this map.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: We are the 30th?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe it's the 31st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 31st.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 31st. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you can find an area with a light background but it doesn't matter. This is fine.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we remove this exhibit let me ask you, do you remember that the first Cutileiro map envisaged that all these green areas and the sand-coloured areas should be part of a Bosniak Muslim canton and we accepted that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that the valley of the Una and Sana were supposed to be one canton and I believe it should have been called Prijedor-Bosanski Most whereas Kljuc would be outside of it. I believe that Prijedor and Sanski Most were supposed to be one region, the -- that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
