utterances.text: That was the first proposal, but do you remember when the Cutileiro maps came there was no mention that these territories should be contiguous, that they could be separate in different areas?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, we can agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the second proposal, Cutileiro's map envisaged that a large part of Prijedor and large parts of Sanski Most should be part of the Cazin Krajina; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. But Mr. Karadzic I believe that when speaking about this portion of the cantonisation process, if you recall, there was a lot of resistance by the Croats from the HDZ and some other political circles, and I believe there were some disagreements there between the SD -- I don't think the disagreements were between the SDA and the SDS, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you. In the end they did accept this proposal but they were hoping that perhaps they could just join Croatia territorially, so maybe that's why. Well, anyway, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this map, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1835, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, it will be difficult for me to identify the page, but perhaps 220 of Exhibit 3517, but I'm not absolutely certain. Now, on this page you talk about when happened in Prijedor. You provide some examples to point out that there were other places where these things did not happen. [As read] "[In English] At the same time, if you compare these with some other localities in Bosnian Krajina such as Sipovo which had a clear Serb majority and were only -- and were there only about 20 per cent of Bosniak, we see that there were almost no crimes committed in the area with the exception of several individual killings. The similar situation can be found in some other areas of Bosnian Krajina, that is the areas which had a Bosniak minority such as the town of Bosanska Dubica and some others." [Interpretation] Would you agree that to this we could add also Gradiska, Srbac, Laktasi, even Prnjavor, and that in these municipalities other than the opportunistic killings there were no major problems?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you see this green area, Srbica. Can we go back to the earlier image, please. Can you see in Srbac this large green area and would you agree that this is Bosanski Kobas?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. The answer that the witness just gave is: Yes, that's correct. That's what I said. Was he agreeing that he said that apart from Gradiska, Srbac, Laktasi and even Prnjavor, that in these municipalities other than the opportunistic killings there were no major problems or was he agreeing that he said that in relation to Bosanska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you help us, Dr. Mujadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned, by way of example, Sipovo municipality and Bosanska Dubica. As for other municipalities in the area of Bosanska Krajina, I do know that in Laktasi -- or no, rather, in Kotor Varos, there were some problems and also in Laktasi, there were problems. As well in -- as well as in some other municipalities, but we can't go that far and analyse each of the 17 municipalities in Bosanska Krajina, but what I said was in the context of a possible analysis of why there were so many crimes in the Sana River valley where there was a large concentration of Bosniaks and I'm referring to Kljuc, Sanski Most, and Prijedor primarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But Madam Sutherland should have probably put this to you during her cross-examination -- additional examination, but I would -- I will clarify it. Other than these opportunistic killings, there weren't major problems either in Gradiska, or Srbac, Laktasi, or Prnjavor. Can you see that Bosanski Kobas, for instance, remained in that area throughout the period, there was one killing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, put your question one by one. If you make compound questions, you will be worse off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you agreed with me, didn't you, that in the list of municipalities that you listed as examples we could add Gradiska, Laktasi and Prnjavor. In other words, other than opportunistic and individual killings, there weren't major problems or that it couldn't be compared to the situation in the Sana River valley?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure about Bosanska Gradiska, Mr. Karadzic. I believe there were some problems there as far as I can recall, and I believe that there were some difficulties in Laktasi. I believe that Bosanska Dubica had a rather calm period, and I believe that Sipovo fared rather well and I believe I mentioned those municipalities to contrast that with the municipalities in the Sana valley -- Sana River valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that other than one killing where some Ljubomir was killed in Srbac the same thing applies?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. We could agree that Srbac too was rather quiet and peaceful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't need the map any more, thank you. You go on to say in this same part of your testimony that you consider that the Sana River valley was strategically significant for both parties and that is why there was bloodshed there; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I said that the Sana River valley was of strategic significance for the plans of the army -- or, rather, later that would be the Serbian Army. And that's because Banja Luka was a mere 60 kilometres away, which is about 35 to 40 miles from the Sana River valley, and that there was a large concentration of Bosniaks there. I believe some 120.000 to 130.000 Bosniaks live in that area, and that this was the reason why Major Zeljaja was given this special task to cleanse the valley of the Sana River.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, since you already mentioned that, let me ask you this: Who was it who started the fighting in the Sana River valley? Who opened fire first that led then to the developments later on?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, personally I think that this entire operation in the Sana River valley was planned by the military top brass in Banja Luka and that it was precisely implemented and co-ordinated by Major Zeljaja. I also know that Bosniaks were aware that operations of this type are possible and that there were plans for them, and they were very careful not to provide any trigger for -- that would then lead to such an operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but do you remember that in many meetings that you attended you carried out preparations having a view that -- or believing that there will be a war? So can you tell us when the plans of the SDA were drafted?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I can't recall the exact date, Mr. Karadzic, but I believe that I said something to that effect earlier -- early on, but this was more than 15 years ago, so a lot of time has passed. Perhaps you can look at my earlier statement, but I know that this happened after the war broke out in Croatia. So it must have been either in the second half of 1991 or in early 1992, perhaps January or February, but I'm not really absolutely certain and I cannot tell you the exact time or period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we -- I think it's 4647. No. 2906. 1D2906. Do you agree -- or, rather, did you attend this meeting at Dom Milicija on 10th of June, 1991 when, the Council for National Defence or security was established?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see this here. In this interview, you say that this council was established when the Cutileiro Plan went down the drain. Let's just wait for a second and see which page this is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says 51 on that page. I mean in the magazine itself. Can we leaf through it further? I think's page 6. No, no, more than that. This is number 2, whereas we need part 3. Page 10. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this. In the upper left-hand corner --

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Could you zoom in a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please zoom in a bit, the upper left-hand corner. And you say that the war had not started in Slovenia yet. There was a major step forward made, the first serious activities of the Patriotic League started when a meeting was held after the gathering at Dom Milicija after the failure of the Cutileiro Plan. So when the Cutileiro Plan failed, the alliance for national security was established. Is this not a mistake? On the 10th of June there was no war in Slovenia, and there was no Cutileiro Plan. You actually created this alliance, as it were, without any of this having happened.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you please remind me of the date of the Cutileiro Plan? It is possible that I made a mistake in this interview. However, this text was never approved by me at the time, so I'm not sure how much of this is relevant from the point of view of authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, you know that in the West the journalists do not let you give any kind of approval at a later stage. Whatever you said, you said, and that's it. The 13th of February was the first time the Cutileiro Plan was discussed in 1992. However, on the 10th of June, 1991, there was no war in Slovenia, and you said when the war in Slovenia had not even started yet. You said that this was a major step forward, serious activity of the Patriotic League, and that this started on the 10th of June; right? Because the meeting at Dom Milicija took place on the 10th of June.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: As for the organisation of the council for national security. I don't understand what you're trying to say putting this question. The council for national security is a council. Quite simply, it looked at various issues. The Bosniak people were concerned from the point of view of safety and security and I think that such a -- such an institution was supposed to exist anyway. The very fact that a council for national security exists does not imply anything else but the Bosniaks thinking about an institution that would consider the security and safety of the Bosniak people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at what it says here. Certain persons were elected to this alliance at republican level, people from the top leadership, and then this was transferred to regional level. So political and military political nuclei were created that had some kind of political co-ordination, some military staffs at regional level, and then this was transferred to municipal level, and so on. The first specific activities involved a call that Hasan Cengic made. Later on, he would be known as the main coordinator and initiator of the Patriotic League. You say that coordinators of the SDA were invited, you, yourself, were invited and let's see what Rusmir Mahmutcehajic said?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we please see this on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say further down somewhere, first, Rusmir in his introductory statement say what lay if store for us. This was July 1991 and this is what he says verbatim: [As read] "Brothers, what we have ahead of us is a difficult and bloody war. Prepare yourselves, because we will be attacked by the Serb army or the JNA. They will be merciless. They will destroy and torch everything. However, we need to preserve our dignity. We have to behave in accordance with Islamic rules and our own written rules that are no different from the Geneva Convention. We should not kill children ...," and so on and so forth. So do you agree that Mr. Rusmir Mahmutcehajic had no cause to say this on the basis of anything that had actually happened in July 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, can we now have the text on the monitor so that the gentleman can see it? Can we scroll down so the witness can see this?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Rusmir, well, I confirm the authenticity of this having happened, and I confirm that Rusmir spoke along those lines as you said. So this is quite authentic. All of us were surprised, personally speaking, by what he said. He is an historian, a Bosnian intellectual. He is well-versed in history. He had some kind of intuition. He was like a prophet, if you will. Prophet. What was the word?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Prorok" is the word for prophet.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. He knew that this kind of thing would happen, so he prophesied it, and that's what happened. I repeat that this was an individual initiative by Rusmir Mahmutcehajic as an intellectual. However, you know full well that the political leadership of the SDA, including Alija Izetbegovic, kept saying right up until the beginning of the war that a war would not actually happen. You know of these words of Alija's. Like Mahatma Gandhi he spoke about peace; he said that there would be no war. So in a practical terms at that point in time, nothing was happening. In a practical and organisational sense, this is an isolated event when Rusmir Mahmutcehajic, as an independent intellectual, yes, truth to tell at that time, also a member of the SDA, spoke like a prophet and said that it was highly likely that this kind of thing would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will see on this page that some practical steps were taken after all. Let me ask you something else. Is it correct that Mr. Izetbegovic said that because that is what the people wanted to hear and that that was the reason? You said that on the previous page of this interview.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I personally think that Mr. Izetbegovic believed that himself, because I had an opportunity of discussing this with Mr. Izetbegovic myself. We were all aware of the fact that a war could break out, but in our heart-of-hearts we thought that a solution would be found nevertheless and that it would be averted. We were hoping that at the end of the 20th and beginning of the 21st century something like that could not happen in Europe. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Fine. Let us look a bit further down. You describe Sefer Halilovic in the beginning of 1991 -- or, rather, in the beginning of September 1991, Sefer Halilovic came to Prijedor, then Cazin, Cazinska Krajina, and that there was this plan for all of it. The republican staff of the Patriotic League drew up this plan. Can we now have the top of the right-hand column. Changes -- no assessments, professional assessments. They were presented -- just a moment, please. They were for the most part majors, captains, military experts who presented the entire situation, political, military, strategic, et cetera. After Sefer Halilovic was there, Sulejman Vranj came, sometime in the beginning of November, 1991, and his task was to carry out regional co-ordination, to establish co-ordination between the republican staff and regional and Municipal Staffs, and to carry out activities aimed at establishing military staffs. Can we go a bit further down. You say specific tasks are being given. Atif Saronjic, nicknamed Dugi, was given the task of teaching people how to use explosives. That's what written here; right? Sefer conducted political general talks with us, whereas this Saronjic was doing more specific things.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: That is what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just have the previous page now. Oh, all right. No, we don't have to really. We shouldn't waste any time. Can we have the next page now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karadzic, can you read this? I think it's very important to read the sentence that follows the last sentence you had read in the previous article. Could you please do that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Atif Saronjic, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: No, no, the previous article. You read that sentence and then there's another one that follows it, that refers to the platform of the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we upload it again? Yes. Could you read it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just show me where it is and then I'll read it out.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: It says: "We conducted general political talks about whether we accept the Patriotic League having a platform, a broad-based platform, that it should be a broad front of all forces irrespective of faith, ethnicity, that honour the platform of the then Presidency of the BiH that wish to defend Bosnia as an equitable community of all peoples ...," and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I have to skip from one topic to another. You spoke about mobilisation in 1991. Towards the end of the second mobilisation, there were some Chetnik insignia that appeared, and you agree that the Presidency recommended that people do not respond to the mobilisation; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the mobilisation at the time when there was a war in Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. The spring of 1991 and September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the recommendation of the Presidency. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree, or rather, do you know that the JNA or the Army of Republika Srpska did not tolerate Chetnik insignia and that that could have only been some show-business Chetnik?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Maybe that was your official policy, Mr. Karadzic, but the situation on the ground was different. I would like to refer to the previous part of my testimony that has to do with mobilisation, the 5th Kozara Brigade, Colonel Colic and what happened in Jaruge in Kozarac. If that could be found, perhaps? It's explained there in detail why -- actually, that this was not just an individual, Mr. Karadzic. At least in that unit that was a mass phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you just let slip when you said that the Serb Radical Party took part in the elections in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: The Serb Radical Party took part in this coalition with the SDS. I think I explained that. There was this coalition between the SDS and the Serb Radical Party during those elections, and the representatives of the Serb Radical Party were part of the joint list of the SDS and the Serb Radical Party. Mr. Vracar, for example, was on the republican list of members of parliament. Milomir Stakic, himself, was vice-president of the Serb Radical Party. Later on he became vice-president of the SDS when the elections took place once again in the SDS in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the Serb Radical Party was founded in February 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to republic level, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade, it was established in February 1991. Before that, it had not existed. There was the People's Radical Party headed by the lawyer Guberina, but it had a different programme.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I can assure that you in Omarska there was a Serb Radical Party and that Mr. Stakic was its vice-president and Vracar was its president and that the Serb Radical Party was a guest at the founding Assembly of the SDS in Prijedor and Milenko Vracar, who was president of the SDS when the Yugoslav anthem was sung and when everybody got up, he was the only person to remain seated, because he said that was not the anthem of the Serb people. He said that the anthem of the Serb people is "Boze Pravde," and he protested against the anthem of Yugoslavia. I don't know whether you're aware of these details, Mr. Karadzic, but it is beyond dispute that the Serb Radical Party existed in Omarska. Now whether it was official at the level of Yugoslavia or Bosnia-Herzegovina, that's a different question altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This comes as news to the Radicals as well because they could not have been established before the party was established in Belgrade. However, let's leave that aside. On page 52, I assume that this is 3571 plus 2. You said that the Territorial Defences had actually become republican armies; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: That was correct in the case of Slovenia. Later on it became correct in the case of Croatia as well, and partly it became correct in the case of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In other words, for the Honourable Chamber to understand the discussion at the moment, I would like to say that the Yugoslav People's Army underwent a process that started in the early 1980s, around 1985 and 1986, and gradually actually became more and more Serbian. The process was long. And then the 1984 constitution was ignored and that's why the Yugoslav People's Army decided to eliminate the organisation of the Territorial Defence in various republics and place the Territorial Defence directly under its own command and organise it differently, without paying any respect to the republican borders. I explained that in greater detail in my previous testimony, and I said that Slovenia managed to take over the weapons from the Territorial Defence, that no other republic managed to do that. The Yugoslav People's Army confiscated all the equipment and weapons, which means that both Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina had only small nuclei organisation in terms of human resources as the basic cells of the future Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I have to put to you this: Do you agree that decision on the placement of the weapons of the TO was made by the Presidency of the SFRY before the first democratic elections, which means that a decision was taken by the Communist powers?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, this is precisely what I have just mentioned and what I explained in greater detail in the Tadic case. There I spoke about a gradual process which led to the victory on the part of the nationalist forces among the ranks of the Communist league.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please let's not go into any political debate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic -- Mr. Karadzic, do not interfere with the witness when he's answering the question. Please proceed, Dr. Mujadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have specific questions. My question is this: This was not done by our administration. This was done before the election; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said on page 51 when you stopped the JNA convoy in August 1991, in your statement and in your testimony 3571 plus 51, you said that you did that because you believed that the JNA had to be placed under civilian control and that you as an MP stopped the convoy and sought explanation. Do you agree that the civilian control over the army is not something that is in the hands of the republican bodies or federal MPs, it is only the Presidency that has that control?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: I agree with you completely, Mr. Karadzic. The commander of the Yugoslav People's Army was the Presidency of Yugoslavia. However, what I wanted to achieve in that conversation and I explained that in greater detail, was merely information. The population was disturbed by the appearance of the troops and weapons in Prijedor, because they knew what was going on in the neighbouring Republic of Croatia. Again I'm referring you to the Tadic and Stakic case where I explained why people were concerned with such a huge concentration of military force in Prijedor. They were concerned primarily because of the events in Croatia where the Yugoslav People's Army, which, de facto, reacted as a Serbian Army at the time because it already had a 90 per cent lead in Serbian cadre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, on page 55, you say that the Croatian forces crossed over to the Bosnian side and opened fire on Bosanska Dubica, Knezica, for example, 50 kilometres in Prijedor, and that they also instilled fear among the Serbian population?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that Bosnian cities were bombarded from Croatia as well?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I would like you to leave five minutes at the end of today's session. So you have five minutes to continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Five minutes today, Your Excellency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to talk about the initial causes of the crisis in Prijedor. Do you agree that even before the elections you had problems with posters, because the Serbian side wanted a reference to be made to Yugoslavia? Do you agree that the first solemn declaration was in dispute not because the Serbs wanted Serbia -- Yugoslavia to be mentioned first and then Bosnia, but because the Serbs wanted the declaration to be taken in the way it was mentioned in the constitution? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic and Your Honours, I apologise. I've just been asked two questions. Again, I have to ask you whether you agree we take each question at a time. You mentioned two completely different events that had nothing to do with each other. One was in Prijedor and the other was in Sarajevo, the republican level. Can I take events one at a time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but briefly, please. What was the sticking point, in your view?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: As far as the common poster, is concerned and that poster was proposed by us, our proposal was that the three parties, in order to achieve better co-operation and tolerance, to present joint posters and to appear in rallies together. I explained that already in the Tadic and Stakic cases. Those things were absolutely denied by the Serbian Democratic Party, because there was a radical stream represented by Mr. Vracar, and Stakic said they didn't want anything to do with the Turks and Ustashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll withdraw my question about the solemn declaration. Is it true that the agreement about the division of power at the republican level between myself, Mr. Izetbegovic, and Mr. Kljuic was somewhat different from what you did in Prijedor, and you spoke about that on page 66 -- or rather 3571 plus 66 in the transcript that has been admitted,

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the source of the major crisis in Prijedor was the fact that the Serbs were not allocated a seat of -- as the police commander? Do you agree that it was a custom during the socialist era and according to the agreement that we signed that if the chief of police was from one ethnic group, the commander had to be from another ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, and we supported that SDS initiative, but that was not the reason why the agreement was not implemented. We had a conversation in the hallway of the Assembly, and Jovan Tintor was there, Mr. Srdjo Srdic, and yourself and some other people were present, I believe, and I explained to you in great detail why there were discords and why the implementation was halted. I expressed at that moment my personal readiness to agree to any concessions in order to give the Serbian side the security that we don't have any hidden agenda, that we had conceded, and that the Bosniak side should have had about 55 per cent of the power in view of the electoral results. The Croatian Democratic Union had to be given 4 or 5 per cent because they had only two MPs and the Serbian Democratic Party was supposed to be given about 45 per cent however we accepted and our proposal was that the Serbian Democratic Party and the SDA should be given an equal number of positions or -- or seats, and then that both sides should cede a certain number of seats or positions to the Croatian Democratic Union. But I believe, Mr. Karadzic, that you will remember that Srdjo Srdic said, "We will not allow an Ustashi and Muslim coalition." And then I said, "Srdjo, you don't have to worry. If we're going to do that, we will make further concession. I have to consult with my organisational bodies first but I can say that the SDS will be allowed to take 50 per cent and let the SDA and the HDZ share the remaining 50 per cent in order to achieve that agreement." And finally that agreement was implemented and then Velibor Ostojic, who attended the Assembly that was implemented in Prijedor and he had been sent to seal at that deal and implement that agreement. As far as the police commander was agreed, we -- is concerned, we agreed to him being a Serb. We had some technical difficulties. We implored with the Serbian side to give us an adequate candidate. We could not have any influence on that the Serbian candidate proposed, a candidate who was not sufficiently --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My apologies to interrupt, but we have to stop here today. We'll continue tomorrow morning at -- at 9.00. Probably you will be aware of this, but while you're testifying here, you're not supposed to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. Do you understand this, sir? So while we discuss of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- discuss a couple the matters, you may be excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we are seized of a motion from the accused for reconsideration on the ninth suspension with respect to KDZ-456 filed today. Can I expect from you an expedited response by the end of this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Understood, Mr. President. I believe we will be able to achieve that. If there's any reason why not we'll get back to you but we understand that's the Court's request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And further we also note the motion for interviews of Prosecution's -- interviews of Prosecution witnesses filed today or yesterday. Given the urgency, I have requested the registry to file its Rule 33(B) submission, if any, by the end of today. Do you like to respond to that as well, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That information was conveyed to us and we're working on it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 1st day of November, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.44 p.m.,
